## 1 Abstract

This vignette works through the modified HP filter of Choudhary, Hanif
and Iqbal (2014): the smoothing parameter chosen series by series by the
generalised cross-validation of McDermott (1997). It applies the filter
to the US quarterly series of the package, sets the results beside those
of the paper, and shows how the criterion behaves. The data differ from
the paper’s (FRED 1959Q1 to 2009Q3 here; IFS 1957Q1 to 2010Q1 there), so
the values are compared, not reproduced.

## 2 The idea

The HP filter fixes \\\lambda\\ by the frequency of the data: 100 for
annual, 1600 for quarterly and 129600 for monthly series. Choudhary et
al. (2014) argue that one value cannot suit every series and every
economy, and choose \\\lambda\\ for each series as the minimiser of \\
\mathrm{GCV}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{T}\left(1 +
\frac{2T}{\lambda}\right)\sum\_{t=1}^{T}\left(x_t -
\hat{g}\_t(\lambda)\right)^2 \\ over \\\lambda = 1, 2, \dots\\ (their
eq. 6). The vignette “Theory” derives this criterion and its exact form.

## 3 One series

``` r

data(us_macro)
fit <-
  mhp_filter(
      x          = us_macro$gdp
    , max_lambda = 100000
    , as_dt      = FALSE
    , log_scale  = TRUE
    , criterion  = "approximate"
    )
fit
```

    Modified HP Filter Result
    ==============================
    Observations: 203
    Optimal lambda: 683
    GCV: 2.82e-04
    Filtered on the log scale; cycle = series - trend in levels

    Cycle Statistics:
      Mean: 1.044
      SD:   91.54
      AR1:  0.8554
      Range: 561.9

    Sources: Hodrick and Prescott (1997); McDermott (1997); Coe and McDermott
    (1997); Choudhary et al. (2014); Choudhary et al. (2014, MATLAB code). Full
    references: mhp_cite(x).

The criterion against \\\lambda\\ has a single interior minimum:

``` r

ggplot2::autoplot(
    object = fit
  , which  = "gcv"
  )
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

and the trend and cycle:

``` r

ggplot2::autoplot(
    object = fit
  , which  = "decomposition"
  )
```

## 4 Three US series

[`mhp_batch()`](https://myaseen208.com/mhpfilter/reference/mhp_batch.md)
filters the columns of a matrix, each with its own \\\lambda\\.

``` r

X <- log(as.matrix(us_macro[, c("gdp", "consumption", "investment")]))
b <-
  mhp_batch(
      X          = X
    , max_lambda = 100000
    )
lam <- attr(x = b, which = "lambdas")
lam[, paper := c(941, 841, 488)]
lam
```

            series lambda          gcv paper
            <char>  <int>        <num> <num>
    1:         gdp    683 0.0002819926   941
    2: consumption    534 0.0001753795   841
    3:  investment   1009 0.0063778004   488

The column `paper` holds the values of Table 2 of Choudhary et
al. (2014) for the United States. Ours are of the same order, below the
1600 of the HP filter, but differ series by series: the samples and the
vintages of the data are not the same, and the criterion is flat near
its minimum, so small changes in the data move \\\lambda\\ a long way.
Investment has the largest \\\lambda\\ here and the smallest in the
paper.

``` r

plot_batch(
    x         = b
  , show      = "cycle"
  , facet     = TRUE
  , highlight = NULL
  )
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

## 5 Against the HP filter

[`mhp_compare()`](https://myaseen208.com/mhpfilter/reference/mhp_compare.md)
sets the cycle of the HP filter with the conventional \\\lambda\\ beside
the cycle of the modified filter.

``` r

mhp_compare(
    x          = log(us_macro$gdp)
  , frequency  = "quarterly"
  , max_lambda = 100000
  )
```

            method lambda   cycle_sd    cycle_mean       ar1 cycle_range
            <char>  <num>      <num>         <num>     <num>       <num>
    1:          HP   1600 0.01543904  4.942713e-12 0.8668207  0.08590516
    2: Modified HP    683 0.01333176 -1.634336e-13 0.8280266  0.07801575
                gcv
              <num>
    1:           NA
    2: 0.0002819926

``` r

plot_comparison(
    x          = log(us_macro$gdp)
  , frequency  = "quarterly"
  , max_lambda = 100000
  , show_cycle = TRUE
  , fmhp       = FALSE
  )
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

## 6 How stable is the choice?

Because \\\lambda\\ is estimated, it changes as data arrive. Refitting
on samples that end in successive years shows how far:

``` r

ends <- seq(from = 120, to = nrow(us_macro), by = 8)
data.table::data.table(
    T      = ends
  , lambda = vapply(
        X         = ends
      , FUN       = function(n) {
          get_lambda(
              x = mhp_filter(
                  x          = us_macro$gdp[seq_len(n)]
                , max_lambda = 100000
                , as_dt      = FALSE
                , log_scale  = TRUE
                , criterion  = "approximate"
                )
            )
        }
      , FUN.VALUE = numeric(length = 1)
      )
  )
```

            T lambda

## 7 The simulation designs of the paper

Choudhary et al. (2014) compare the filters on 30 simulated designs: a
random-walk trend with drift and an AR(2) cycle, with six pairs of AR
coefficients and five ratios of the standard deviations of the two
shocks. `mhp_designs(paper = "2014")` lists them and
[`mhp_simulate()`](https://myaseen208.com/mhpfilter/reference/mhp_simulate.md)
draws a series from one of them; the vignette “Simulation” runs the
comparison.

``` r

mhp_designs(
    paper = "2014"
  )
```

## 8 References

Choudhary, M. A., Hanif, M. N. and Iqbal, J. (2014). On smoothing
macroeconomic time series using the modified HP filter. *Applied
Economics*, 46(19), 2205–2214.

Hodrick, R. J. and Prescott, E. C. (1997). Postwar U.S. business cycles:
an empirical investigation. *Journal of Money, Credit and Banking*,
29(1), 1–16.

McDermott, C. J. (1997). An automatic method for choosing the smoothing
parameter in the HP filter. Unpublished manuscript, International
Monetary Fund.
